title: Room and Winter
premise: Quentin Hartwell, a hospice nurse who has heard the dying count backwards for seven years, takes a live-in post at Wrenfield House, where an elderly matriarch, her estranged daughter, and a grieving grandson are keeping vigil over a dying father. When every mirror in the house begins reflecting the room one second late, Quentin realizes the backwards counting is not a symptom of dying but a summons — something on the other side of the glass is counting down to the harvest moon, when it will harvest the whole family. To save them, Quentin must discover why she alone can hear the count, break a bargain her own dead mother made decades ago, and lead the family out of the house before the moon rises — even though crossing back through the mirrors means leaving someone behind.
about_author: Ada Iversen is a former night-shift caregiver from coastal Maine who writes horror about the quiet hours when houses seem to breathe. She lives in a drafty farmhouse with two cats and a mirror she refuses to hang facing the bed.

chapters.title: The Count
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. On her last shift at Rosewood Hospice, Mr. Ellery counts backwards from thirty as he dies, and Quentin writes it off as terminal lucidity — until his lips keep moving after his heart stops. She accepts a lucrative live-in nursing post at remote Wrenfield House, telling herself distance will quiet what she hears. Emotional beat: dread disguised as practicality.

chapters.title: Wrenfield House
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. She arrives through fog to a house of shuttered rooms and covered mirrors, meeting matriarch Vivian, her brittle daughter Lorna, and ten-year-old grandson Toby, who asks immediately whether she hears them too. The dying father, Aldous, sleeps upstairs behind a door painted with salt lines. Emotional beat: unease wrapped in professional calm.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. At 3 a.m., Quentin catches her reflection in the hallway mirror lagging a half-second behind her movements. By dawn, every uncovered glass in the house reflects one full second late. Vivian orders the mirrors re-covered; Lorna calls Quentin hysterical. Emotional beat: the first crack in seven years of rationalization.

chapters.title: What Aldous Counts
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Sitting vigil, Quentin hears Aldous counting backwards in his coma — not from thirty, but from nine thousand and something. Toby, eavesdropping, admits he hears it too, and that the number is smaller every night. Emotional beat: the terrible intimacy of sharing a secret with a child.

chapters.title: Lorna's Ledger
chapters.summary: Lorna's POV. Lorna has kept a ledger of family deaths going back four generations — each one preceded by a backwards count and a 'late' mirror. She believes the house is owed something and intends to pay it with Aldous alone. Her chapter reveals love curdled into transactional survival. Emotional beat: guilt sharpened into strategy.

chapters.title: Vivian's Bargain
chapters.summary: Vivian's POV. In 1974, young Vivian found her mother bargaining with something in the glass to save Vivian's dying brother — a bargain renewed by each generation's eldest woman. Vivian has been renewing it for fifty years, and the thing in the mirror has begun asking for more than one life. Emotional beat: duty as a slow-acting poison.

chapters.title: Toby's Friend
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Toby introduces Quentin to 'the lady in the wall,' who shows him pictures in the darkened TV screen — including a woman who looks exactly like Quentin, younger, wearing a nurse's uniform from another decade. Quentin recognizes her mother's face. Emotional beat: vertigo of personal history intruding on the present.

chapters.title: The Harvest Moon Almanac
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Researching in the attic, Quentin finds a farmer's almanac annotated across a century: every harvest moon marked with names, each name struck through except three — Vivian, Lorna, Toby. The countdown in Aldous's room now stands under forty. Emotional beat: the plot becomes a deadline.

chapters.title: Salt and Silence
chapters.summary: Lorna's POV. Lorna reinforces the salt lines and forbids Toby from the east wing, lying to him that his grandfather is improving. That night the mirrors reflect the hallway a second late — and then, briefly, a figure standing in the reflected hall that isn't in the real one. Emotional beat: protective lies beginning to cost more than truth.

chapters.title: Mother's Uniform
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. In a locked cedar chest, Quentin finds her mother's hospice uniform and a letter unfinished: 'If you can hear them counting, you were chosen before you were born.' Quentin learns her mother once worked at Wrenfield House — and left mid-count, abandoning the family to the bargain. Emotional beat: inherited debt, inherited cowardice.

chapters.title: Aldous Wakes
chapters.summary: Aldous's POV (brief, dreamlike). Aldous surfaces from the count long enough to tell Quentin the truth he's held since his own mother's death: the thing in the glass doesn't take the dying — it takes whoever the eldest woman loves most, and it always offers a trade. He begs her not to let Vivian trade again. Emotional beat: a dying man's last act of protection.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Vivian's POV. The mirror shows Vivian her long-dead brother, whole and warm, offering renewal of the bargain: one beloved soul at moonrise, and the rest of the family lives untouched forever. Vivian, exhausted by fifty years of payments, almost says yes — and looks at Toby sleeping in the reflected room. Emotional beat: temptation wearing a loved one's face.

chapters.title: Broken Glass Logic
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Quentin tests the lag: objects thrown at mirrors land a beat after their reflections shatter. The reflection-world isn't showing the room late — the room is showing the reflection early. Something over there is already happening first. She realizes the count isn't a warning; it's a rehearsal. Emotional beat: horror reframed as physics.

chapters.title: Lorna Breaks
chapters.summary: Lorna's POV. Confronted with Quentin's evidence and her mother's confession, Lorna shatters the great hall mirror in fury — and the shards each show a different room, all of them counting. The house groans; doors open onto wrong halls. Breaking the mirror didn't stop the bargain; it opened every window at once. Emotional beat: rebellion backfiring into catastrophe.

chapters.title: Sixteen
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. The count reaches sixteen. Power fails, phones dead, the road out dissolving into fog that exists only inside the property line. Quentin organizes the family around one plan: reach the old chapel on the grounds before moonrise, where her mother's unfinished letter says the count was once interrupted. Emotional beat: leadership forged from fear.

chapters.title: What the Lady Wants
chapters.summary: Toby's POV. Guided by the lady in the wall — who Toby realizes is trying to help, not haunt — the family navigates the shifting house. She shows Toby the truth: she is Quentin's mother, trapped in the glass since she fled in 1991, and the only way out for everyone is a willing substitute. Emotional beat: a child carrying an adult's impossible message.

chapters.title: The Chapel Count
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. In the chapel, Quentin finds her mother's final entry in the parish register: the count can be broken if someone on this side answers it forwards — speaks the numbers up instead of down, refusing the summons. But answering means standing in front of a mirror when the count reaches zero. Emotional beat: courage defined as staying put while everyone else runs.

chapters.title: Moonrise
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs interwoven. The harvest moon clears the treeline. Every remaining reflective surface floods white; the count reaches five. Vivian tries to offer herself; the glass refuses her — it wants the one who hears best. It wants Quentin. Emotional beat: sacrifice colliding with self-preservation.

chapters.title: Answering Forwards
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Quentin steps before the great mirror and counts aloud — one, two, three — against the falling numbers, her mother's voice joining hers from inside the glass. The two counts collide at the midpoint; the reflection-world stutters, loses its half-second advantage, and begins to crack. Emotional beat: love against duty, resolved as defiance.

chapters.title: The Price
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. The bargain demands its due: the glass takes a Hartwell. Quentin's mother steps through instead, trading her fifty years of captivity for release — both directions at once, unmade and free. The mirrors go dark, then ordinary, reflecting on time. Emotional beat: grief and liberation in the same breath.

chapters.title: Room and Winter
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Weeks later, Aldous dies naturally at dawn, counting nothing at all. Vivian, Lorna, and Toby ask Quentin to stay — not as staff, but as family. She unpacks her bags in a room with no mirror, and hangs one small photograph face-down. Emotional beat: found family chosen in the aftermath of loss.

chapters.title: Coda: What the Dying Say
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV, years later. Back at hospice work, Quentin still sits with the dying — and sometimes they murmur numbers, but now she holds their hands and counts gently upward alongside them until the numbers stop. In her pocket, a note in her mother's handwriting: 'Answer forwards.' Final emotional beat: peace negotiated with the dark, one voice at a time.
